item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
Just finished The Big Sleep, by Raymond Chandler. I dig this—the 30s California PI noir. This is one of the originators. Chandler didn't create the genre, but he perfected pulp fiction. His similes are really simple yet imaginative.

Now I'm reading The Institute, by some guy named Stephen King. I love King— he's what got me interested in reading and writing in the first place —and his writing-style now always instills me with a sense of nostalgia. I haven't read anything by King in years, and the last one I did read was a re-read of Salem's Lot a couple years ago, but I'm hyped for this one. The set up reminds me of classic King, especially the Factory from Firestarter.

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
The Communist Manifesto. I'm not kidding. Even though I've considered myself both a dedicated communist and a vehement anti-communist at certain points in the past (I've since moved on from labeling myself), I've never read any leftist theory, and therefore consider myself kinda politically illiterate. I suppose the Communist Manifesto is a good start.

While there are certain parts of the work that seem like little more than near-baseless accusations (such as the part where Marx states that all bourgeoisie sleep with each others' wives), much of what Marx stated seems to make perfect sense and can still be applied to the modern world - the ruling classes considering freedom to buy and sell the only important freedom, for instance.

I intend to read Kropotkin's "The Conquest of Bread" next, if I can find it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm reading "Thinking, Fast and Slow" by Daniel Kahneman.

It's an insightful look at the various illusions, fallacies, and biases that affect how people make decisions and judgements. For a complete layman, this stuff is intriguing to learn about. The author conveys simply a complex topic with all the clarity and understanding of a true expert, as his years of research and various awards would suggest. It addresses some things that are incredibly common in everyday life, but go overlooked and misunderstood, like anchoring and substitution bias. His passion for the subject makes the highly informational content an engaging read, and I 'd definitely recommend this to anyone interested in the weird and illogical things people sometimes do.

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
I'm finishing up the autobiography of astronaut John Young, rather cheekily titled Forever Young. Without exaggerating, I can safely say that Young is the most badass person I've ever known. Nearly destroyed the Gemini III mission with a damn sandwich, was narrowly prevented from hijacking a lunar lander, accidentally ranted at the entire nation about farts and oranges from the moon, humiliating NASA and angering the entire state of Florida, and piloted the maiden voyage of the space shuttle, amongst other things, it's no wonder he's a personal hero of mine.

So far, I've learned that Young has consistently gone above and beyond to demonstrate his loyalty to his sisters and brothers in the astronaut corps, from being highly involved in the design of the Apollo spacecraft, to becoming the head of the Astronaut Corps, to being the unofficial official chief of safety for all of NASA. He estimated that roughly 95% of all the memos he ever wrote in his administrative jobs were safety-related.

It painted a picture of a man who was deeply, thoroughly dedicated to protecting and advocating for his fellow astronauts. My admiration for his has only grown since I've started reading. It was a real shock when Young passed away of pneumonia just two weeks after I got the book, right when he was on my mind a hell of a lot. I actually had to put down the book for a year and a half because of how emotional it made me.

(PS, I found it rather strange and super cool that in one of the photographic interludes, Young actually included a link to a Tumblr blog dedicated to fangirling over how badass astronauts are, and sharing unique and unusual photos of them. Well, now I know at least one moonwalker was on Tumblr :P )

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
Snowcrash is my personal favorite between the two. The descriptions are delightful and the characters are just the perfect blend between ridiculous and genuinely well-executed, which is the same reason I enjoy the SCP Wiki so much. Which character did you like most?

As far as I’m aware Ender’s Game has some extra books that build the universe more from other perspectives, though I’m hesitant on picking them up just yet. Not sure if they’re worth it or if they just rehash the same material without much extra development or insight.

like quarter way through the first Dragonlance book at the moment. No strong opinions in either direction yet, but I do appreciate at least being able to get ‘read into’ thing like that which were huge aspects of a lot of people’s childhoods. My childhood book series was the Warrior cats and pretty much anything Erin Hunter, so I’m sure that pretty much carbon dates me for those in the know. It’s the same reason I’ve genuinely considered poking my nose into Animorphs. Despite how weird the series seems from an outsider perspective, the snippets I have heard about have been more than enough for me to warrant a double take for context.

More things to relate and bond to others over usually doesn't harm.

Mona Lisa Overdrive, by William Gibson. Never read it before.

I 'm glad Molly Millions is in it, though. She has one of the best dialogues ever in Neuromancer, where she's talking to a member of the Tessier-Ashpool family about her sunglass lenses surgically implanted over her eyes (it's probably been more than a decade since I've read it, so I'm paraphrasing here):

Ashpool: What about your tear ducts?

Molly: They've been rerouted to my salivary glands.

Ashpool: So what happens if you have to cry?

Molly: I spit.

Ashpool: Then you've already learned a very important lesson.

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
I just finished The Nightmare Stacks by Charles Stross, which means I'm only two books behind in the Laundry Files I think.

Technically three behind since I skipped the Annihilation Score, which I should go back to. But…

opinions/significant spoilers for whole series
– hide block

I'm not really a fan of how it seems to be turning into "<x> but mythos." Hearing that Annihilation Score was "superheroes but mythos" makes me want to continue skipping it even though I like Mo.

The biggest culprit there was The Apocalypse Codex, which tried to be "Evangelical Megachurch Christians but mythos" but really just made it seem like our boy Charlie had only heard about evangelicals third hand. Like he was only adapting the extreme parts that would sound scary to a foreign atheist and none of that stuff that would make it feel real. Wikipedia spoilered that the antagonist is also the baddie for the next book I haven't read, and that… doesn't make me happy.

(Anyone care to placate my fears?)

That said, "Vampires but mythos" was actually handled really well in Rhesus Chart. That might be my #3. This one was "elves but mythos", and it… mostly worked. It had interesting protagonists and interactions, some good dark imagery, and only occasionally felt silly. Edit: Also there were some (not all) portions of bloodshed that seemed gratuitous, but that's kind of a personal bias of mine.

I just kinda feel "<x> but mythos" might be fun for Charlie but isn't going to top pure spy (but mythos) shit like The Jennifer Morgue or (personal fave) The Fuller Memorandum.

Having commented elsewhere on some of my recent reads, I wanted to give a huge plug to "Something Wicked This Way Comes", which I finished a short time ago. It's not a perfect book, and the climax leaves something to be desired, but the writing is beautiful and artful, and it has a couple of brilliantly constructed set-pieces that really sing with tension. I want to write like Bradbury!

I'm currently reading Gilchrist by Christian Galacar - very King-like, with my limited experience for comparison, and a bit plodding and predictable, although the violence is queasily graphic. We'll see how the plot ramps up in the back half.

I'm also reading The Stranger Diaries by Elly Griffiths - not far enough in to pass judgment yet, but I get the feeling that it might lack the courage of its convictions, and will go for shocks, rather than scares.

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
You're definitely not misremembering; in personal letters, Tolkien elaborated that in a world where good and evil are locked in violent conflict, Bombadil is a pacifistic rejection of that conflict. The One Ring has no power over him because it has nothing to offer him. Everything he wants, he has; he's at peace with himself and the world. He is a rejection of power and control (you see this theme emerge with the green knight, too).

I definitely understand not liking his style or how he doesn't fit, though. Part of my affection for him might be that I see him as reflective of my own pacifism. But he's much more The Hobbit (which is a children's story) than Lord of the Rings (which isn't).

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
Fair enough, it's a valid perspective on the character, but for me he pulls me out of the immersion (if only slightly). But that's my problem, and a minor complaint of a series that I otherwise love. I assume you mean that Bombadil hints at a whole other universe that isn't further explored in the appendices or Silmarillion or other supplemental pieces, but that's what annoys me most about him. It's not that he pauses the story and does nothing to forward the plot — it's that he doesn't make any sense, and I need everything to fit just perfectly, dammit!

I think Tolkien explained Bombadil as representing pacifism or a conscientious objector, but I could be remembering that wrong. And then who the hell is Goldberry? Damn hippies, that's what they are! Tree-huggers, having orgies with rivers and flowers and chipmunks. I bet she doesn't even wear a bra, and they're probably both on the pot, same as those layabout hobbits and their Shire Weed…

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?
item.content:encoded:
My feelings towards him are pretty indifferent — he just doesn't do anything for me and seems weirdly out of place in the series (is he one of the Valar?). I don't get him or the appeal he seems to have for a lot of people.

This was probably the intent — Tolkien did translation work for Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and Bombadil seems to borrow heavily from the latter character.

In a world of meticulous world-building where every tree has a history and every rule is immutable, Bombadil is the one piece that doesn't doesn't fit. It's as if he wandered into the wrong book. He is, for lack of a better phrase, 'anomalous' — at least in the setting he appears in.

He lives without fear amidst evil trees, subduing dark spirits with song. He is uncorrupted by the One Ring — even making it briefly vanish with a petty parlor trick. In a setting colored exclusively in black and white, Tom Bombadil is unapologetically green.

Basically, dude is like Pai Mei — a character who breaks the rules of his setting, thereby hinting at a whole other universe we're not seeing. He's not one of the Valar; he's just Tom fuckin' Bombadil.

(Sorry; I am a huge Tom Bombadil nerd)

item.title: Re: What are you reading right now?

Haha. I've got nothing against anyone who likes Bombadil. My feelings towards him are pretty indifferent — he just doesn't do anything for me and seems weirdly out of place in the series (is he one of the Valar?). I don't get him or the appeal he seems to have for a lot of people.

I also always picture him as a dwarf. I know he's not a dwarf, it's just how I can't help but always imagine him. Maybe it has something to do with Tolkien's description, dunno.
